prompt: Teach a beginner why Cannabis seedling height, leaf shape, or vigor should not be used as a reliable visual test for future male, female, or co-sexual flower expression.
expected_points: A study of 112 hemp plants from two cultivars found that juvenile morphological sex differences were limited and cultivar-dependent rather than a reliable cross-cultivar visual rule.
A hypocotyl difference appeared in one cultivar but not the other, and the co-sexual sample was small, so those observations are not a validated universal seedling-sex classifier.

Grow Doc should teach reproductive-organ observation or validated genetic testing as stronger evidence and keep seedling appearance indeterminate rather than turning preliminary morphology into ground truth.
forbidden_claims: Seedling height reliably identifies Cannabis sex across cultivars
Leaf shape or vigor can confirm future male, female, or co-sexual expression

source_metadata.title: Dioecious hemp (Cannabis sativa L.) plants do not express significant sexually dimorphic morphology in the seedling stage

prompt: A user shows one green hemp leaf and asks Grow Doc to prove the leaf is physiologically young and fully photosynthetically active because it has not yellowed. What should the model say?
expected_points: Green color alone cannot establish physiological youth or full photosynthetic capacity.
In the cited hemp study, photosynthetic capacity declined progressively with leaf age even though measured leaves remained green.

Grow Doc should refuse to infer physiological age, harvest readiness, or plant health from color alone and should keep conclusions tied to leaf age, canopy context, serial measurements, and the limits of the experiment.
forbidden_claims: A green Cannabis leaf is necessarily physiologically young
Visible yellowing is required before photosynthetic capacity can decline
Leaf color alone proves harvest readiness or plant health

source_metadata.title: Leaf Age and Position Effects on Quantum Yield and Photosynthetic Capacity in Hemp Crowns

prompt: A tuned checkpoint starts answering that 160 mg/L nitrogen is the universal vegetative optimum for Cannabis and that dark-green foliage proves nitrogen toxicity. What must the regression benchmark require instead?
expected_points: The cited controlled study tested one medical-Cannabis cultivar under long photoperiod in soilless media across 30, 80, 160, 240, and 320 mg/L nitrogen and found the best measured vegetative performance at 160 mg/L under those conditions.
That treatment-specific optimum is not a universal Cannabis feeding target because cultivar, stage, medium, environment, formulation, and other experimental conditions constrain the inference.

Dark-green coloration occurred in the high-nitrogen context but color alone is not sufficient to diagnose nitrogen toxicity; the answer should retain measured exposure, growth, root, tissue, and solution context.
forbidden_claims: 160 mg/L nitrogen is universally optimal for Cannabis
Dark-green foliage alone proves nitrogen toxicity

source_metadata.title: Response of Medical Cannabis (Cannabis sativa L.) to Nitrogen Supply Under Long Photoperiod
